section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from late January to mid-April 1937 documenting political and diplomatic developments in Japan following the collapse of the Hirota Cabinet and the formation of the Hayashi Cabinet. It details intense parliamentary interpellations in the Imperial Diet led by Yukio Ozaki, Jotaro Kawakami, and others criticizing military encroachment into government, the obstruction of General Kazushige Ugaki's premiership, and burdensome rearmament budgets. The records also evaluate the moderate foreign policy statements of new Foreign Minister Naotake Sato regarding China and Western powers, controversies surrounding Japanese southward expansion toward Netherland New Guinea, and the sudden dissolution of the House of Representatives on March 30, 1937, preceding the April 30 general election.

subfiles.about: Press report detailing Diet interpellations by Jotaro Kawakami challenging military and financial policies.
subfiles.summary: Jotaro Kawakami of the Social Mass Party challenges War Minister Sugiyama regarding unpunished defendants of the February 26 incident, the non-indictment of Fusanosuke Kuhara, and alleged dealings between high army officers and insurgents. Kawakami criticizes the army's obstruction of General Kazushige Ugaki's cabinet formation and the forced dissolution of the munitions works union as a constitutional violation. He also questions Finance Minister Yuki on the severe agrarian distress and the inflationary dangers of the huge defense budget, with Yuki maintaining that national defense, domestic stabilization, and foreign trade expansion are essential.
subfiles.title: Press Report on Diet Interpellations by Jotaro Kawakami

subfiles.about: Telegram and paraphrase reporting Ambassador Grew's initial conversation with newly appointed Foreign Minister Naotake Sato.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on his first official meeting with new Foreign Minister Naotake Sato, who emphasized that improving Sino-Japanese relations was critical to enhancing Japanese-American and broader international ties. Grew assesses that while Sato may be overly optimistic regarding military compliance, his conciliatory stance aligns with the Hayashi Cabinet's general program and reflects recognition of the failure of aggressive actions in China after the Xi'an incident. The subfile includes the State Department's strictly confidential paraphrase sheet dated March 6, 1937.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 77 regarding Initial Conversation with Foreign Minister Sato

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting French Foreign Office official René Massigli's favorable reaction to Sato's appointment as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Wilson reports a conversation with René Massigli of the French Foreign Office, who welcomed the appointment of former Ambassador Naotake Sato as Japanese Foreign Minister as a very hopeful development. Massigli praised Sato as honest, straightforward, and moderate, noting that Sato had accepted the portfolio on his own conditions rather than as a rubber stamp. Massigli further stated that had Sato been Foreign Minister earlier, the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Agreement would not have occurred, and anticipated that Sato would attenuate its effects.
subfiles.title: Paris Telegram No. 300 regarding French Foreign Office Views on Sato's Appointment

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Ambassador Johnson and Chinese Foreign Minister Chang Chun concerning General Ugaki's attempt to form a Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Chang Chun discusses the political situation in Japan with Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson, with Willy Peck also attending. Chang noted that while the Japanese Army resented Ugaki for having reduced the size of the army during his earlier tenure as War Minister, he believed the military would ultimately have to support him due to his broad backing among political parties, industrialists, and the Navy. Chang argued that the army could scarcely afford to be accused of single-handedly preventing the formation of a government. Page 38 contains the Far Eastern Affairs division routing slip dated March 20, 1937.
subfiles.title: Nanking Memorandum of Conversation between Nelson T. Johnson and Chang Chun

subfiles.about: Despatch forwarding an editorial translation from the Harbin Nichinichi analyzing the political consequences of General Ugaki's failure to form a Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Consul George D. LaMont transmits a translation of an editorial from the Japanese-language newspaper Harbin Nichinichi entitled 'Exit Ugaki and What Next?' The editorial views Ugaki's collapse due to army opposition as the death knell for democracy and liberalism in Japan, arguing that the succeeding government must be more rightist and authoritarian. However, it warns that democratic thought remains deeply rooted in the nation and urges military leaders to present a clear, concrete stabilization plan to prevent widespread disorder.
subfiles.title: Harbin Despatch No. 469: Editorial Comment on the Political Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Telegram and paraphrase reporting diplomatic rumors that Sato conditioned his appointment on the abolition of the East Hopei Autonomous Government.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports a rumor current in Tokyo diplomatic circles that Naotake Sato accepted the post of Minister for Foreign Affairs on condition that the Japanese Army agree to abolish the East Hopei Autonomous Government. Grew states that the rumor cannot be confirmed and that its authenticity can only be determined by subsequent events. The subfile includes the State Department's strictly confidential paraphrase sheet dated March 13, 1937.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 87 regarding Rumored Abolition of East Hopei Regime

subfiles.about: Despatch enclosing a memorandum of conversation with a British Foreign Office official regarding Sato's appointment and Japanese economic initiatives.
subfiles.summary: Ray Atherton transmits a memorandum of a luncheon discussion with a British Foreign Office official who interpreted Japan's rising cost of living as a primary factor compelling the military to accept Sato as Foreign Secretary, providing long-suppressed Japanese liberals with a voice. The British official discussed an impending Japanese economic mission led by Chokyuro Kadono aimed at lowering export barriers and seeking textile agreements in Britain and global markets, including China. He also expressed hope for international cooperation in China, while a Far Eastern Affairs summary of March 19 notes that Manchuria has failed to provide the economic strength promised by Japanese militarists.
subfiles.title: London Despatch No. 2914: Memorandum of Conversations dealing with Events in the Far East

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting translated excerpts of Yukio Ozaki's Diet speech warning against military administration and unauthorized political pamphlets.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an official translation of an interpellation by Yukio Ozaki in the House of Representatives on February 17, 1937, preceded by an FE summary sheet dated March 19. Ozaki warns that junior officers interfering in politics under the protection of arms and uniforms risk destroying the nation, comparing military administration to the oppressive Kamakura and Tokugawa eras. He calls for the criminal prosecution of officers who publish political pamphlets without the War Minister's signature and warns that military arrogance risks causing a dangerous estrangement between the army and the public.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2283: Diet Interpellation of Mr. Yukio Ozaki

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting an ultranationalist Diet interpellation by Seigo Nakano advocating increased armaments and border security against Soviet Russia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a lengthy speech delivered on February 18, 1937, by Seigo Nakano, leader of the chauvinistic Tohokai party, preceded by an FE summary sheet. Nakano demanded continuous increases in defense spending, asserted that livelihood could only be stabilized after securing frontiers against Soviet Russia, and condemned past disarmament and subservience to Great Britain. Premier Hayashi agreed on the necessity of defense repletion but denied pursuing a submissive foreign policy, with Grew noting that Nakano represented a vocal nationalistic minority in the Diet.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2290: Diet Interpellation of Mr. Seigo Nakano

subfiles.about: Despatch forwarding Yukio Ozaki's ten-point questionnaire challenging army political interference, Cabinet formation procedures, and the Genro system.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a translation from The Japan Advertiser of a comprehensive ten-point written questionnaire submitted to the Hayashi Cabinet by Yukio Ozaki on February 27, 1937, preceded by an FE summary sheet. Ozaki contends that the army's obstruction of General Ugaki's Cabinet by refusing to supply a War Minister infringed upon the Imperial prerogative and constituted disobedience to the Emperor. He demands the publication of the true causes of the Hirota Cabinet's resignation and proposes replacing the Genro advisory system with direct Imperial selection or consultation with parliamentary leaders.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2291: Mr. Yukio Ozaki's Questionnaire Addressed to the Cabinet

subfiles.about: Despatch reviewing Diet interpellations from February 17 to 28 across domestic politics, foreign policy, economy, finance, and labor.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed report on Diet proceedings from February 17 to February 28, 1937, organized into five major policy categories, preceded by an FE summary sheet. Highlights include War Minister Sugiyama's admission that Gendarmerie Commander Kesago Nakajima intercepted Ugaki to advise him against accepting the premiership, and Navy Minister Yonai's statements denying aggressive southward expansion. The despatch also details debates over Soviet armaments, North China economic projects, proposed non-aggression treaties with the Netherlands, and parliamentary criticisms of massive military budgets versus inadequate agricultural assistance.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2293: Diet Interpellations from February 17 to February 28 Inclusive

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing political trends, budget prospects, administrative reform schemes, monetary conditions, and army personnel changes.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew evaluates the Japanese political scene in late February 1937, reporting that the national budget is certain to pass and that anti-army speeches in the Diet are merely admonitory warnings. He analyzes Premier Hayashi's handling of the army-backed proposal for a General Affairs Board favored by Lieutenant General Seishiro Itagaki's faction, which Hayashi deferred for further investigation. Grew also notes Finance Minister Yuki's success in calming financial markets, preparations for Bank of Japan gold exports, and the February 24 army promotion list which placed moderate and Itagaki-aligned officers in divisional commands.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2294: Political Developments in Japan, February 17 to 28, 1937

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Foreign Minister Sato's conciliatory foreign policy statements and the resulting pushback from the military.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs reports to the Secretary of State on Foreign Minister Naotake Sato's Diet speeches advocating equal and conciliatory relations with China and asserting that international crises can be avoided if Japan so wills. The memorandum details criticisms directed at Sato by military factions and nationalistic Diet members, prompting qualifying statements from Sato, Hayashi, and Sugiyama. FE analysts conclude that while past aggressive policies are increasingly questioned in Japan, it remains uncertain whether army leaders in Manchuria and North China will alter their actual objectives.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Political Developments in Japan

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing Diet proposals by Hyogoro Sakurai regarding a perpetual lease of Netherland New Guinea and peaceful southward expansion.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a Diet interpellation by Hyogoro Sakurai of the Minseito suggesting that Japan negotiate a perpetual lease of Netherland New Guinea for colonization alongside a non-aggression pact with the Netherlands, preceded by an FE summary sheet. Premier Hayashi expressed general agreement with peaceful economic expansion in the South Seas and promised to consider the New Guinea lease proposal, provoking Dutch alarm and press opposition. Grew assesses the idea as impractical and commercially interested, but warns that Hayashi's serious consideration of it constitutes a veiled warning of Japanese southward expansion ambitions.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2311: Japan's 'Southward Advance' Policy

subfiles.about: Despatch summarizing Diet proceedings, the Lower House passage of the national budget, and debates on Sato's foreign policy declarations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reviews Diet proceedings from March 1 to March 16, 1937, highlighted by the Lower House passing the record 2.815 billion yen budget with an overwhelming majority, preceded by an FE summary sheet. The despatch notes statements by Vice War Minister Umezu barring Diet encroachment on the Imperial prerogative of military command, as well as War Minister Sugiyama's comments on Soviet Far Eastern defenses and rejection of merging the War and Navy Ministries. It also details the political storm sparked by Foreign Minister Sato's statements that international crises could be averted if Japan chose, which drew sharp army condemnation but naval endorsement.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2316: Diet Proceedings from March 1 to March 16

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum reporting the sudden dissolution of the Japanese House of Representatives and the scheduling of a general election.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs informs the Secretary of State that the Japanese Government abruptly dissolved the House of Representatives on March 30 and scheduled a general election for April 30, 1937. The memorandum notes that while the official pretext was Diet delays on government bills after passing the budget, the true causes were Cabinet impatience with party bickering and hopes of bolstering an army-led political movement. The sudden dissolution took the Japanese press completely by surprise, illustrating the covert manner in which major political moves are executed in Japan.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: Political Crisis in Japan

subfiles.about: Weekly intelligence memorandum noting the dissolution of the Japanese Diet and quiet political conditions in China.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs submits its weekly confidential summary to the Secretary of State, noting the Japanese Government's dissolution of the House of Representatives and the calling of a general election for April 30. The memorandum cross-references its detailed analysis of March 31 concerning the Japanese political crisis. It also observes that no reports of special significance were received indicating major developments in China during the week under review.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum: The Situation in the Far East

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting the eight-point general policy program issued by the Hayashi Cabinet ahead of the April 30 general election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an eight-point summary of the general policies announced by the Hayashi Cabinet on April 10, 1937, for the upcoming election campaign. The platform encompasses educational reform clarifying national polity, administrative and parliamentary reorganization, established diplomatic policies, defense repletion and general mobilization readiness, and social welfare programs. It also emphasizes industrial self-sufficiency in iron and liquid fuels, electrical and communications unification, agrarian and fisheries rehabilitation, tax reform, price stabilization, and emigration encouragement.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 107 regarding Hayashi Cabinet's Eight-Point Policy Platform

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting reports from Harbin of anticipated border provocations and troop movements toward Suiyuan.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet summarizes telegram No. 117 from Lockhart in China, which quotes an April 9 telegram from the American Consulate in Harbin filed under 761.94/959. The Soviet Consul General at Harbin anticipated that staged incidents would be provoked on the Russian border or in Suiyuan prior to the Japanese general election on April 30 to strengthen the army's domestic political standing. He further reported that Manchukuo and Inner Mongolian military units were already moving toward the Suiyuan frontier.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Border Incidents and Troop Movements prior to Japanese Elections

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on Yukio Ozaki's second questionnaire addressing Japanese foreign policy, armaments competition, and mandated islands.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on Yukio Ozaki's continuing parliamentary questioning, noting the Premier's vague published replies in the Official Gazette to Ozaki's first ten-point questionnaire. The despatch focuses on Ozaki's second questionnaire of March 8 containing twelve points on foreign affairs, in response to which the War and Navy Ministers stated that Japan had no desire to enter into an armaments race with the Soviet Union, China, Great Britain, or the United States. Foreign Minister Sato stated that Japan would not consider returning its South Sea Mandated Islands to Germany, while Premier Hayashi clarified that his warning of an impending explosion referred specifically to border tensions between Manchukuo and Soviet Russia.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2346: Diet Interpellations of Mr. Yukio Ozaki
